page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.g5.large is a general-purpose virtual machine based on KVM virtualization. The instance provides 2 vCPUs derived from a single dedicated physical core via hyper-threading on a 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon 8163 processor (x86_64 architecture). It includes 32 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 33 MB L3 cache per core cluster, with instruction support including AVX, AVX-512F, AES, and BMI2. Memory is provisioned at 8.0 GB, maintaining a balanced 1:4 CPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include bundled local storage or dedicated GPU hardware accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached block storage. Baseline network bandwidth is configured at 1 Gbps with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses assigned.

Benchmark measurements position the compute and memory subsystems primarily in the entry-tier performance bracket. The instance achieved a Geekbench single-core score of 944.0 and a multi-core score of 1114.0. PassMark results reflect similar constraints, with an overall CPU score of 1822.26, a memory score of 990.16, and a database operations score of 542.48. In stress-ng evaluations, single-core CPU throughput reached 1101.29 while multi-core scaled to 1453.18. Single-threaded gzip compression registered at 18.92 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression achieved 7.47 GB/sec. Large uncached memory bandwidth sustains 10.25 GB/sec for reads and 9.61 GB/sec for writes.

Service throughput metrics record static web serving at 1.31 GB/sec and Redis SET operations at 1.53 million operations per second. Small 135M-parameter language model testing yields 123.69 tokens per second for prompt processing and 37.01 tokens per second for text generation. These performance tiers highlight clear operational tradeoffs: the single underlying physical core limits concurrent compute capacity under intensive parallel loads, and uncached memory throughput remains modest.

The ecs.g5.large instance represents a resource-balanced, cost-conscious tier suited for lightweight enterprise workloads where extensive CPU concurrency is unnecessary. Primary fits include low-traffic web serving, development environments, small background jobs, microservices, and modest Redis caching nodes.
